title: Shortest Paths with Dijkstra
summary: Shortest paths when edges have weights - why BFS no longer works, relaxation, Dijkstra's algorithm with a priority queue and lazy deletion, its O((V + E) log V) cost, rebuilding routes, why negative weights break it, Bellman-Ford and negative cycles, 0-1 BFS, and choosing the right shortest-path algorithm.

cards.q: Why can Dijkstra's algorithm finalise the vertex with the smallest tentative distance?
cards.a:
With no negative weights, no other route is shorter

Any other route to it passes through a vertex at least as far away. This is exactly the step that negative weights break.

cards.q: A popped heap entry (d, u) has d > dist[u]. What should Dijkstra do?
cards.a:
Skip it: the entry is out of date

A better distance for u was found after this entry was pushed. That is lazy deletion: stale entries are simply ignored.

cards.q: Bellman-Ford still improves a distance on its V-th pass. What does that mean?
cards.a:
A negative cycle is reachable

Without negative cycles, all shortest paths are settled after V - 1 passes; an improvement after that comes from a negative-weight cycle reachable from the source.
